messages.subject: Word cloud for keywords
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

was wondering whether anybody knows of R code to create a word cloud (see packages tm, SnowballC, and wordcloud) *for keywords*.  As far as I can see, the usual procedure for word clouds is just based on frequency lists of single texts/text collections. Keyword analysis by contrast involves highlighting those items that are unusually more frequent in a target corpus than in a reference corpus.

Anybody aware of R code available for this purpose?

All pointers appreciated

Chris

--
PD Dr. Christoph Rühlemann
Vertretungsprofessur
Englische Sprachwissenschaft
Institut für Anglistik und Amerikanistik

messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] Highlight data points in stripchart
messages.body_plain:
there are several ways to do this depending on the ploting package you're using. In ggplot the easiest is to create an additional factor variable for your data, where the particular data points you want to highlight receive a different value from the rest. Then you set the "color=VAR", where VAR is the new variable. In base graphics I guess you could just replot the particular data points you want to emphasize.

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Highlight data points in stripchart
messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] Highlight data points in stripchart
messages.body_plain:
You can set the color equal to a vector for a 1D stripchart, just as one would do with the col variable using the plot function. As in plot, the ifelse trick can be useful to do it on the fly (or you can pre-compute the variable as done further below).

str(airquality)  # dataset already loaded by R
stripchart(airquality$Temp, col = "gray",
           bg = ifelse(airquality$Temp > 80 & airquality$Temp < 90, "red", "black"),
           pch = 21,
           xlab = "Temp (F)")

However, this does not work if you are plotting by group due to stripchart deficiencies, apparently. If you are doing by group then you may need to re-plot the points or use ggplot2, as suggested. Because when I try to color by a factor variable using stripchart, it seems to mess up the indices and colors the wrong points. I think it is grouping things internally differently from how it is using the color indices.

airquality$HighTemp <- airquality$Temp > 80
stripchart(Temp ~ Month, data = airquality, vertical = TRUE,
           col = "gray",
           bg = ifelse(airquality$HighTemp, "red", "black"),
           pch = 21,
           xlab = "Temp (F)”)

I’d honestly use ggplot2, but for stripchart this page looked useful: http://www.programiz.com/r-programming/strip-chart

And this SO answer explains the stripchart coloring really well, including how you need bg to color the points as opposed to col: http://stackoverflow.com/a/22923960

Alex

messages.subject: Latent Semantic Analysis for text files comparison
messages.subject_clean: Latent Semantic Analysis for text files comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am currently working on a corpus made of 23 .txt files. I would like to plot the results of a Latent Semantic Analysis to see how similar each file is to the others.
To do so, I have tried following the instructions provided by Cheng at the following URL:
http://meefen.github.io/blog/2013/03/11/analyze-text-similarity-in-r-latent-semantic-analysis-and-multidimentional-scaling/
and made use of the tm, lsa and ggplot2 libraries.

I think I messed with the file loading process, since I get the following error message when running the TermDocumentMatrix function:

Error in UseMethod("meta", x):  no applicable method for "meta" applied to an object of class "character"

and

Warning message:  In mclapply(unnamed(content(x)), termFreq, control) : all scheduled cores encountered errors in user code.

May I ask your help to solve this problem (or find an alternative way)?

Thank you in advance,
Claudio

___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Further info about the files:

Each file contains contains 1m Italian tokens.
The corpus represents 23 different semantic domains.
As mentioned in Cheng's blog, stopwords, punctuation and numbers are removed in the preprocessing stage.
